news.2026-11-07-chine-rencontre-xi-trump: Xi, Trump and Putin at the same table? Beijing confirms talks for the first time, possibly in Shenzhen

Beijing has confirmed for the first time that a meeting between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin is under discussion. Nothing is settled: it could take place on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen on 18 and 19 November, and analysts doubt it will produce concrete results [1][2][3].

This week, Chinese diplomacy acknowledged publicly for the first time that it was considering the idea of a meeting between the Chinese, Russian and American leaders. It says it remains in contact with "the parties concerned"; its spokeswoman Mao Ning, quoted by US media, spoke on the subject [2][4].

The Kremlin had paved the way on 3 November by saying such a summit was under discussion [3]. According to information picked up by the press, it was Vladimir Putin who reportedly proposed the idea to Donald Trump during a call on 9 October [1][2].

Nothing is fixed, neither the date nor the venue. The most frequently cited possibility is a meeting on the sidelines of the APEC (Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation) summit scheduled in Shenzhen from 18 to 19 November [1][2].
According to a source cited by the Financial Times and relayed by the media, Washington and Moscow are both pressing Beijing to agree [2].

Analysts interviewed by the AP news agency doubt that the three leaders, whose interests clash, will agree on anything concrete: the meeting could mainly serve as a photo opportunity [1]. Donald Trump said he would rather talk about nuclear arms control than about Ukraine [2].

Key takeaway: if it happens, NBC calls it a "historic" meeting: the leaders of the United States, Russia and China have never met all three together. China's confirmation shows that Beijing is willing to place itself at the center of the diplomatic game [1][2].

For Europe, the stakes are direct: Ukraine could be discussed without Europeans at the table. A three-way summit without the EU would raise the question of Europe's place in talks that concern it first and foremost.

On the economic side, the timetable is tight: the trade truce between Washington and Beijing, rare earths and sanctions against Russia are all tied to the relationship between these three capitals. A gesture of détente (or a failure) in Shenzhen could move oil prices, stock markets and supply chains.

If you live in Europe, what is decided between Washington, Moscow and Beijing affects your energy, your prices and the continent's security, even if Europe is not invited. Next to watch: the APEC summit on 18-19 November.

news.2026-11-07-ue-chine-coupe-circuit-p: EU-China trade: Beijing threatens to retaliate against Europe's "kill switch", and Xi calls himself Europe's "partner"

On Thursday in Brussels, China's ambassador to the EU threatened retaliation if the Union adopts unilateral measures against Chinese interests. The next day in Beijing, Xi Jinping repeated to Christian Stocker, the Austrian chancellor, that China is not the source of Europe's problems [1][2][3].

On 5 November, at the 14th China-Europe Forum in Brussels, China's ambassador to the EU, Cai Run, warned that Beijing would retaliate if the Union adopted measures deemed discriminatory. He did not specify the nature of the countermeasures [1].

Brussels is preparing a tool nicknamed a "kill switch" that would let it react quickly when a third country's decision seriously disrupts its market. According to Euronews, France and Germany called for it in early October [1].
EU leaders have also asked the Commission for measures (quotas, tariffs) against Chinese imports in chemicals and machinery [1].
The imbalance is massive: Euronews cites €559.4 billion of Chinese goods imported by the EU, against €199.6 billion exported to China [1].

On Friday 6 November in Beijing, Xi Jinping received Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker. According to Chinese state media, he said China is "a partner and a fellow traveler" that can help Europe, not the cause of its difficulties, and called for trade frictions to be settled through dialogue [2][3].

Christian Stocker replied that Austria supports the development of EU-China relations and wants both sides to settle their differences through frank discussion. Beijing proposes cooperating with Vienna on AI, electric cars, digital technology and the green economy [3].

Key takeaway: China is sending two messages at once, an outstretched hand to Vienna and a threat to Brussels. It hopes that the countries least dependent on its imports will weigh against joint European measures [1][3].

The economic context explains the tension: Chinese exports hit a record $447.18 billion in September 2026 (+36.3% year on year), including chips up more than 108%, according to Al Jazeera. European chemicals and machinery manufacturers see this cheap merchandise coming [4].
For the EU, the challenge is to defend its factories without triggering a trade war: Beijing weighs heavily in the supply of European industry, which makes any escalation risky for both sides.

If you work in industry (chemicals, machinery, automotive) or buy Chinese products, this standoff may affect prices and jobs in Europe. A European kill switch would mostly take the form of tariffs or quotas at the border.

news.2026-11-07-fmi-zone-euro-regles-bud: The IMF warns Europe: loosening the eurozone's budget rules further would be a mistake

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) believes the eurozone should tighten its management of public finances rather than relax its budget rules, while countries hit by the energy crisis, including Giorgia Meloni's Italy, are calling for more flexibility [1].

On Friday 6 November, Euronews reported the IMF's warning against a further loosening of the eurozone's budget rules. The institution believes the Union should instead consolidate its public finances [1].
An excessive deficit procedure, with an adjustment of 1.5%, is already in place across the bloc, with leeway granted for defense spending [1].
The countries hardest hit by the energy crisis, including Giorgia Meloni's Italy, are asking for more flexibility [1].

In a report presented in Bangkok on 16 October, the IMF estimated that about three quarters of European countries needed to tighten their budget discipline, with an average adjustment of about 3.5% of GDP, whereas the plans negotiated with the Commission provide for about 2% on average [2].

The debt market is already under strain: the yield on the French 10-year OAT rose as high as 5.07% intraday on 21 October, according to Saxo, and the spread with the German Bund has stayed well above 100 basis points since late September [3][4].

Key takeaway: two logics are at odds. On one side, governments that want to spend to cushion the energy shock and rearm; on the other, the IMF, which fears that an overly loose framework will push up the rates at which states borrow [1][2].

European budget rules serve to reassure lenders: they limit the deficit and debt. When investors doubt a country, they demand a higher rate to lend to it, and the debt burden rises, which is the case for France at the moment [3][4].

The debate also affects the ECB, which does not face the same urgency when states borrow more: if governments stimulate, the central bank may have to raise its rates harder against inflation (4% in October in the eurozone).

If you are a French citizen, these rules partly determine the state budget, and therefore taxes, public services and the rate on your future mortgage. If Europe loosens, debt climbs; if it tightens, the bill may fall on public spending.

news.2026-11-07-france-quatrieme-samedi-: France: fourth Saturday of protests against the high cost of living, two days before the social conference at Matignon

About a hundred demonstrations are planned this Saturday 7 November in France against the high cost of living and for young people, for the fourth Saturday in a row, two days before the social conference announced by Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu [1][2].
According to Euronews, about a hundred rallies are organized this Saturday across the country, the fourth consecutive Saturday of protests [1].

In Paris, the intersyndicale (CGT, FO, FSU, Solidaires, CFDT) and youth organizations (Union étudiante, Fage, Unef, USL) are calling for a march between République and Nation from 2 p.m., under the slogan "against the high cost of living and for young people" [2].
The yellow vests, for their part, are maintaining an unauthorized rally at place de la Concorde [2].
Thursday's day of action had brought together about 350,000 people in Paris according to the CGT and 65,000 according to the Interior Ministry: the gap between the two figures remains enormous [2].
On Monday 9 November, Sébastien Lecornu brings unions and employers together at Matignon for a social conference, with no minimum wage increase decided at this stage [1].

Key takeaway: the protests are lasting because prices weigh on households and the government's response is not yet known. The unions are coming to the social conference with a show of strength: four Saturdays and a major strike day within five days [1][2].
Students and high schoolers are joining the movement: this is what differs from the usual strikes, as young people are raising the issues of rents, the cost of living and employment [2].

For the executive, the room for maneuver is narrow: the trade deficit and French debt worry the markets, which limits the spending increases (wages, aid) it can grant without further damaging the budget.
If you live in France, these protests may lead to decisions that directly concern you: minimum wage, housing aid, energy prices. The marches may also disrupt transport this Saturday in Paris.

news.2026-11-07-ukraine-zelensky-madrid-: In Madrid, Zelensky asks Latin America for transformers and cables to save Ukraine's power grid

Visiting Madrid on the sidelines of the Ibero-American summit, Volodymyr Zelensky made an urgent appeal to Latin American leaders: transformers from Brazil, Mexico, Argentina and Colombia, cables from Chile, generators from Spain, to prevent the collapse of Ukraine's grid [1][2].
Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Spain this week for the 30th Cumbre Iberoamericana and met head of government Pedro Sánchez [2][3].

Before the region's leaders, he asked for help "as quickly as possible" to save Ukraine's power grid from incessant Russian attacks. He is seeking transformers (Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, Colombia), cables (Chile), generators and electrical equipment (Spain) [2].
He asked governments to put his teams in direct contact with manufacturers to speed up deliveries, as the equipment must match Ukrainian grid standards [2].

He also met King Felipe VI, to whom he offered his condolences after the rail collision near Toledo, and spoke with UN Secretary-General António Guterres. On the military front, he again called for Patriot missiles [2].

According to Euronews, Argentine President Javier Milei boycotted the opening ceremony and the state dinner, and came only to the plenary session, a snub to host Pedro Sánchez, three weeks before Spain's general election on 29 November [2].
On the ground, new Russian strikes hit Kyiv this Saturday: five injured, a bridge and energy infrastructure damaged [4].
Key takeaway: Ukraine is widening its search for aid beyond Europe and the United States. Latin America produces transformers and cables, and these parts are lacking in Kyiv as winter approaches [2].

The visit also shows the divisions in the Western camp: Milei, close to Washington, snubs the ceremony of a left-wing government, a reminder that the war in Ukraine gets mixed up in each country's internal political quarrels [2].
The issue is economic: each strike on the grid costs Ukraine industrial output, activity and exports, and pushes allied countries to finance equipment rather than weapons.
If you live in Europe, a Ukrainian grid brought down pushes millions of additional refugees to flee westward this winter. It also weighs on the demand for financial aid from the EU.

news.2026-11-07-fin-rebond-ia-wall-stree: Wall Street, United States
Rebound after the AI crash
After the AI crash, Wall Street rebounds, but insurance against credit defaults soars: warning signals remain orange

After Thursday's drop (Nasdaq 100: −6.4%, $2.3 trillion in market capitalization wiped out), Wall Street rebounded on Friday, but the fear index remains high and the rise in default insurance is, according to Reuters, the clearest warning signal [1][2][3].

On Thursday 5 November, the Nasdaq 100 fell 6.4% to 26,629.81 points, according to Saxo, or about $2.3 trillion of market value wiped out according to NBC and Yahoo Finance. The Nasdaq Composite lost 5.31% and the S&P 500 4.24% [1][2][3].

On Friday, the Nasdaq 100 regained nearly 2% (Reuters); the S&P 500 finished at 7,376.86 points (+0.31%) according to Yahoo Finance, while the Dow Jones fell about 0.4% after a US jobs figure stronger than expected, which pushed yields up [2][3].
The VIX, the fear index, had topped 28 on Thursday, its highest since late March, up more than 40% over the week according to Reuters; it fell back to 24.31 on Friday [2][3].
According to Reuters, stress indicators are at orange without being at red. The most worrying is credit: investors are buying far more insurance against borrowers defaulting on payments [2].

Chips rebounded: AMD gained 10.77% after the previous day's fall [4]. Press coverage links the fall to the midterm elections: a Democratic Congress could scrutinize the AI sector more closely and slow the construction of data centers [2].
Key takeaway: a one-day rebound settles nothing. Markets saw that a large part of their recent gains rested on AI, and the question is whether the rise was justified by earnings or by enthusiasm [2].

Credit is the barometer to watch: when investors buy protection against defaults, they fear that companies heavily indebted to fund their AI investments will struggle to repay. Reuters notes, however, that the VIX jump remains modest compared with that of August 2024 or April 2025 [2].
Interest rates matter too: solid US employment pushes up yields, and therefore the cost of credit, which weighs on stocks whose profits are expected far in the future.

If you have life insurance, a PEA or a world ETF, you indirectly hold these tech giants: their fall shows up on your statement. To understand, not to decide: high volatility is no reason to advise buying or selling.

How it works: the VIX and default insurance

The VIX measures the volatility investors expect on the S&P 500 over the next thirty days: it is derived from the price of options, that is, insurance contracts against a decline. When fear rises, this insurance costs more and the VIX climbs [2]. Credit has its own barometer: "credit default swaps" (CDS), contracts that pay the buyer if a borrower does not repay. If their price rises, investors see a greater risk of bankruptcy. When the VIX and CDS rise together, the panic does not stay in equities, it affects corporate financing [2].
Precedents: when fear spread through the markets
5 August 2024
The VIX tops 65 intraday, its highest since 2020, and the Nikkei loses about 12% [5]. The Bank for International Settlements attributes the stress to the unwinding of yen-funded "carry trades" [6].
A panic of a few days caused by market technicalities (positions funded in yen): the storm subsided quickly [6].
3 April 2025
After the announcement of the "Liberation Day" tariffs, the S&P 500 plunges 4.84% in one session; it does not turn positive for the year until 13 May [7].
It took about six weeks to erase the year's loss: the shock came from trade policy, not from an earnings problem [7].

news.2026-11-07-maroc-gasoil-aide-transp: Morocco: diesel is rising again, and the government extends aid to transporters

The Moroccan government announced on Monday 2 November the continuation of its exceptional and direct support to transporters, for fifteen more days, as the price of diesel has risen again since 1 November [1][2].

The new tranche of aid covers an additional period of fifteen days, for professionals in road passenger and freight transport. Registration opens on 10 November on a dedicated electronic platform, according to the MAP agency [1][2].
Diesel has cost more since 1 November. The aid, reactivated in March 2026 amid tensions in the Middle East, does not directly change pump prices: it compensates transporters, not motorists [2][3].

The scheme has existed since 2022; the cumulative amount paid is said to be close to 11 billion dirhams, according to the Minister of Transport and Logistics [3]. Operators remain worried about how long this support will last [3].

Key takeaway: Morocco imports its fuel, so the Middle East crisis shows up directly in its prices. By paying transporters, the state prevents the rise in diesel from being passed on to the price of vegetables, fruit and travel [2][3].
The budgetary cost builds up, fifteen days after fifteen days: this is the limit of this policy.
If you have family in Morocco or travel there, transport and fresh produce prices depend on this aid. For a French reader, it is an example of what the oil crisis does to an importing country.

news.2026-11-07-algerie-tomate-280-dinar: Algeria: tomatoes at 250-280 dinars a kilo, a price surge that has lasted since September

In Algeria, good-quality tomatoes sell for between 250 and 280 dinars a kilo in wholesale and retail markets, according to Maghreb Émergent. The rise began in September and is not slowing, despite a state plan to bring prices down [1][2].
According to Maghreb Émergent (4 November), good-quality tomatoes reach 250 to 280 dinars a kilo in markets, and 260 to 280 in fruit and vegetable shops. The outlet speaks of a "historic" surge [1].
The rise began in September and is not slowing, again according to the Algerian outlet [1].
Algérie360 mentions a state plan to bring down the price of tomatoes, after the kilo exceeded 280 dinars [2].

Key takeaway: the tomato is a staple of Algerian cooking, and its surge shows up directly in household budgets. The government is stepping up measures (capping the price of potatoes at 90 dinars a kilo in early October, according to RFI) to contain food inflation [2].
The word "historic" is the outlet's: the sources do not all date this wave precisely, and other episodes of sharp increases have already occurred.
For a French reader, this is a reminder that rising food prices also affect the southern Mediterranean, just like the rise in fresh produce in Europe.

news.2026-11-07-perou-depasse-chili-pib-: Latin America: Peru is about to overtake Chile in economy size, according to the IMF
According to the IMF's October projections, Chile's nominal GDP ($402.2 billion) is now only $2.65 billion ahead of Peru's ($399.6 billion) in 2026, and Peru would move ahead in 2027 [1][2].
In the IMF's 12 October update, Chile's nominal GDP stands at $402,243 million and Peru's at $399,593 million, a gap of $2,650 million [1][2].
For 2027, the IMF projects $413,597 million for Peru, against $413,443 million for Chile: Peru would move ahead, narrowly [2].
Growth explains the catch-up: in 2026 the IMF forecasts +3% in Peru and +0.6% in Chile (versus 2.4% announced in April for the latter), then +2.9% and +2.6% in 2027 [2][3].

Key takeaway: Chile has been ahead for almost forty years; 1989 is the last year Peru had overtaken it, according to a Peruvian outlet [2]. The headline of the Chilean daily La Tercera on 7 November states it bluntly.
Caution: nominal GDP says nothing about per capita living standards, which remain higher in Chile [2].
If you follow the global economy, this shows that countries rich in copper and ores do not all benefit in the same way from commodity prices: Peru, more stable, is catching up with its neighbor.
news.2026-11-07-espagne-urda-parquet-eur: Spain: after the Urda train collision, the European Public Prosecutor's Office investigates possible fraud involving Madrid-Seville line funds

The European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) has opened an investigation into possible fraud involving European aid intended for the renovation of the Madrid-Seville high-speed line, after the Urda collision near Toledo. No fraud has been established at this stage [1][2].

According to Euronews, the EPPO is looking for irregularities in the use of European funds earmarked for modernizing the line. Investigative measures are being carried out at the headquarters of Adif, the public network manager, and at other public bodies. The prosecutor's office has not named any company or contract [1][2].
A first proceeding on the same line had been opened in March, after the January accident in Andalusia, which killed 46 people [1].

The death toll cited for the Urda collision is 69. Media outlets disagree on the date of the accident (28 October or 2 November), and the press notes that the financial suspicions are not linked, at this stage, to the technical causes [1][2].

Key takeaway: Spain has received billions of euros in recovery funds for its infrastructure, and a rail tragedy raises the question of oversight of that money. The European investigation shows that Brussels is monitoring the use of its funds [1][2].
The issue is political: the accident occurs three weeks before the 29 November general election, which makes the case sensitive for the government.

If you take the train in Europe, the investigation is a reminder that safety depends on line maintenance, and therefore on money invested in infrastructure. For European taxpayers, it is a matter of the proper use of EU funds.

news.2026-11-07-france-intemperies-corse: Corsica: two dead in floods, a couple's car swept away between Porto-Vecchio and Bonifacio
Two people over 70 died in the night from Thursday 5 to Friday 6 November in Corse-du-Sud, after their car was swept away by floods. The Gard and Hérault were also hit by the bad weather [1][2].
According to the prefecture, the car, carrying three people, was swept away around 1 a.m. on the RT10, between Porto-Vecchio and Bonifacio. Their daughter survived [2].

The prefecture sheltered 80 people in a Porto-Vecchio gymnasium and activated a crisis unit. Rescuers carried out 43 interventions during the night and brought 32 people to safety in the south of the island [2].

According to Météo-France, the worst of the bad weather seemed to have passed on Friday morning, as the disturbance shifted toward Italy. An earlier episode, on 20 October, had already caused casualties in Corsica [2].

Key takeaway: violent Mediterranean episodes keep recurring in the south of France, with a human toll and damage to roads and homes. Two deadly episodes in less than three weeks in Corsica reignite the debate on prevention and compensation [1][2].
For insurers and the state, each episode adds to the bill of the natural disaster scheme.
If you live in or travel through the south of France in autumn, these episodes develop quickly: in case of orange or red alert, avoid the road and never drive through a flooded area.
news.2026-11-07-chine-loi-anticorruption: China: Beijing adopts a law against cross-border corruption, and companies will have to set up a compliance department

The Standing Committee of the National People's Congress adopted a law against corruption beyond borders on Friday 6 November, the Xinhua agency said. It extends Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign and requires Chinese companies to create compliance functions [1].
According to Xinhua, the law aims to deepen international cooperation against corruption and to protect the country's sovereignty and security [1].
Chinese companies will have to set up anti-corruption compliance functions [1].

The text has six chapters and 47 articles: institutional mechanisms, handling of cases, international cooperation, duties of integrity and compliance, legal liability. It aims to fill legal gaps around corruption linked to activities abroad, to recover illicit assets and to strengthen oversight of Chinese companies operating outside the country [2].

The draft had first been reviewed in August, at the 24th session of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress; the date of entry into force does not appear in the sources consulted [2].
Key takeaway: China is equipping itself with a legal tool to pursue people and funds abroad, which may complicate life for foreign companies that work with it [1].
For European groups established in China, compliance becomes one more issue, alongside trade tensions with the EU.
If you work for a company with partners or subsidiaries in China, new compliance obligations may apply to contracts and payments.
